articles.title: Building a freight CBM and chargeable-weight calculator: the edge cases nobody warns you about
articles.excerpt: I work at a freight forwarder in Shenzhen, and most of the questions we get before a quote are some version of "why is my shipment billed on more kilos than it weighs?". So we built a calculator: ente…
articles.body: I work at a freight forwarder in Shenzhen, and most of the questions we get before a quote are some version of "why is my shipment billed on more kilos than it weighs?". So we built a calculator: enter your cartons, get the volume, the volumetric weight, and how each of our shipping lanes would actually bill them. The arithmetic looked like a one-liner. It wasn't. This post walks through the model we ended up with in TypeScript, and the edge cases that broke the first versions. The three numbers everything starts from Every carton has outside dimensions in centimetres, a count and a gross weight. From those you get: Volume (CBM) : L × W × H ÷ 1,000,000 , times the number of cartons. Volumetric weight : L × W × H ÷ divisor .

articles.title: Building an Android AI Agent, Part 15: Session Memory Without Storing Sensitive Data
articles.excerpt: Building an Android AI Agent, Part 15: Session Memory Without Storing Sensitive Data In Part 14 we handled context misfires — cases where AgentContext builds a confident but wrong model of what the us…
articles.body: Building an Android AI Agent, Part 15: Session Memory Without Storing Sensitive Data In Part 14 we handled context misfires — cases where AgentContext builds a confident but wrong model of what the user is doing. This part covers a different problem: memory across sessions. Right now, every time the user opens StareBrain, the agent starts fresh. It knows what's on screen. It knows recent app switches. It doesn't know that this user always drafts emails before sending them, or that they use a specific task app to close out their day, or that "send the doc" always means the most recently edited file in Google Drive. That kind of pattern is useful. It shouldn't require the agent to watch you fail and recover a dozen times before it learns it.

articles.title: Being first to market no longer matters. So why is everyone rushing?
articles.excerpt: Decades ago, when I sat in front of investors to sell my new idea, the first question was: why won't Microsoft just do it itself? I have to explain the Microsoft question, or any other giant in the fi…
articles.body: Decades ago, when I sat in front of investors to sell my new idea, the first question was: why won't Microsoft just do it itself? I have to explain the Microsoft question, or any other giant in the field, because today it sounds a bit funny. The conception back then was that whoever gets to market first is king, and the more technological power a company has, the better its chances of success. The challenge of making an idea succeed was seen as a technological one, not a market one. A lot of water has flowed under the bridge since. To begin with, the giant companies are no longer seen as competitors but as potential acquirers. There are almost no technological challenges left in development, and in most cases vibe coding does the job quite well.

articles.excerpt: Most landing page problems aren't design problems. They're handover problems. The marketer assumes the developer set up tracking. The developer assumes the marketer tested the form. The page launches,…
articles.body: Most landing page problems aren't design problems. They're handover problems. The marketer assumes the developer set up tracking. The developer assumes the marketer tested the form. The page launches, ad spend starts, and a week later someone notices the conversions report is empty, or the form has been sending leads to an inbox nobody reads. A shared checklist fixes most of this. Not a long one: four areas, each with a few checks, and a name next to each. Here's the one I'd want both teams to sign before any paid traffic goes to a page. 1. Speed A slow landing page wastes the money spent getting people to it. Paid visitors are the least patient visitors you have. Test on a mid-range phone over mobile data , not just a fast laptop on office Wi-Fi.

articles.title: Hackers used Chrome and Snapdragon GPU flaws to hack Android phones
articles.excerpt: A nasty Chrome bug let hackers break into Android phones without a tap.
articles.body: TL;DR A security firm has found that hackers exploited a Chrome bug and a Qualcomm Adreno GPU driver flaw to infect Android phones that visited a booby-trapped website. The attack targeted Chrome versions 139 to 145 on Android and stole browser cookies, saved logins, browsing history, and Wi-Fi passwords. Both flaws had already been patched, so phones running up-to-date Chrome and security updates remained safe. Security researchers at Sekoia have detailed a mobile hacking campaign that went after Android and iPhone users through hijacked and fake websites. On Android, the attackers didn’t need victims to tap a link, install an app, or grant a permission. Opening an infected page in an outdated version of Chrome was enough.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 4, 2015: A rail-launched Super Strypi rocket carrying 13 baby satellites failed during its debut launch for the US Air Force
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 4, 2015, the United States Air Force launched an experimental Super Strypi rail-launched rocket carrying 13 tiny satellites, but it failed just after liftoff from Hawaii.
articles.body: On Nov. 4, 2015, the United States Air Force planned to launch an experimental rocket for small satellites from the Pacific Missile Range Facility off Barking Sands, Kauai, Hawaii. The launch didn't according to plan . For this mission, the Air Force was testing out the Super Strypi rocket . The rocket used a rail to help with the liftoff. Super Strypi left the ground, but the rocket quickly spun out of control. When it crashed, it destroyed all of the tiny satellites riding aboard the rocket. The cause? Likely a problem with the first stage motor. The mission lost 13 tiny satellites known as cubesats. Cubesats are a popular option for space missions, because they are small and cheap, and they often operate in swarms.

articles.title: Hackers exploited iOS and Android flaws to infect phones
articles.excerpt: Researchers say group may have been Kremlin-sponsored in search of diplomatic targets.
articles.body: Hackers possibly linked to the Kremlin exploited previously patched iOS and Android flaws in an attempt to hack visitors of multiple websites, including one celebrating the 250th anniversary of American independence, researchers said Wednesday. The attackers, which the researchers assessed with “moderate to high confidence” were part of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service, targeted other sites, many with links to that country’s ongoing war against Ukraine. The attacks began when iPhone or Android users visited one of potentially hundreds of different sites. JavaScript injected into the traffic then profiled the device. The final payloads, tailored to the type of platform visiting, attempted to steal browser cookies and, in some cases, Wi-Fi passwords and full mobile device data.
